open-question.question: What alternative text does the banner image carry in the four READMEs: an empty alt marking the image as decorative, or a short description of the arms, and in that case what wording?
open-question.applied-principle: Check tier claims against the live environment
open-question.recommendation: GitHub wraps every README image in a link, so an empty alt would leave a link with no name for a screen reader to announce, while a few literal words name it, follow the written-alt pattern of every badge on the pages, and stay true however the count, size, or palette is tuned; the wording is the option's own example, "Octopus arms drawn in ASCII art".
open-question.alternative: The banner carries one short literal description of the picture, identical in all four READMEs, naming only what is drawn and how, with no colours and no counts — for example "Octopus arms drawn in ASCII art" — and nothing of the project's name or tagline. Tells anyone who cannot see the image what is there in a few words, follows the written-alt pattern the badges already set, and stays true whatever arm count, size, or palette the sibling questions settle, so it needs no rewording when the drawing is tuned. Read aloud before the title on every page, it adds a line a screen-reader user hears ahead of the project's name for an image that conveys no information; the words "ASCII art" hold only while the art's character set is limited to ASCII, which the art-character-set question decides.

The banner's image element carries no alt attribute at all in any of the four READMEs: no text is written for it, empty or otherwise, and what a screen reader or a failed image load shows is left to the browser. Nothing to word or keep in step across the four files, so the banner's line in each README is the shortest it can be. Breaks the pattern every image on the four pages follows today, each badge carrying a written alt such as "Latest Release" or "unique views"; screen readers commonly announce the file name or URL in its place, and a broken load shows nothing that says what was meant to be there.

The banner carries an empty alt (alt="") in all four READMEs, marking it as decorative so assistive technology skips it and the page's spoken reading starts at the badges, then the title. Matches what the banner is for a non-sighted reader: pure ornament ahead of a title that already names the project, so nothing redundant is read before the "# Gurita" heading, and no wording has to track the drawing's arm count, characters, or colours as those are settled or later changed. A sighted reader whose image fails to load, and every screen-reader user, learns nothing of the banner at all; it is also the one image on the pages with no written alt, so the choice reads as an omission unless it is understood as deliberate.

The banner carries one fuller literal description, identical in all four READMEs, stating what is drawn, how it sits, and its colours — for example "Octopus arms curling up from the bottom edge, drawn in violet and grey-blue characters" — still naming neither the project nor the tagline. Gives a non-sighted reader or a failed load the closest equivalent of the picture, its shape and its palette included, which is the whole of what the banner adds to the pages. The longest text read ahead of the title on every page, and every detail it names (the colours, the curling from the bottom edge, any count) becomes a fact the alt must keep in step with the drawing by hand in four files; its wording depends on how the palette, arm count, and character-set questions are settled.

The banner carries the project's name as its alt in all four READMEs — "Gurita" in each, treating the banner as the project's logo — with no description of the arms. Follows the common convention for a header image standing in as a logo, needs no wording to track the drawing's details, and gives a failed load a sensible label. Each page's next heading already says "Gurita" ("# Gurita" or "# Gurita for <Host>"), so a screen reader hears the name twice in a row, and the text says nothing of what the image shows.

The banner carries the tagline "Decide first, then let the arms carry the work." as its alt in all four READMEs, describing the image by the metaphor it illustrates rather than by its appearance. Ties the picture to the meaning the earlier rename mission gave the arms, so a reader who cannot see the banner still gets what it stands for, and it brings that line to the three host pages, which carry no tagline today. On the root README the same sentence stands as bold text just under the title, so it is read twice there; on the host pages it adds the tagline the finished rename mission deliberately kept off them, and it does not say what the image actually depicts.

open-question.question: Is the host suite run on all three hosts as part of this mission, since adding the banner to each host's README template changes every host's trigger set and the suite first requires each host's installed copy to equal the built tree, or is that run left to the next release's pre-flight?
open-question.recommendation: The release pre-flight runs the suite on all three hosts against the same final state before anything reaches a host page, so a closing run inside the mission would only repeat it shortly before, and deferring keeps the task run unattended and the home-directory installations in the maintainer's hands.
open-question.alternative: The mission does not run the host suite at all and ends without one. The run is left to the next release's pre-flight step g, which diffs each host's trigger set since the last tag and so selects all three hosts. Installed copies are refreshed then, by the maintainer, as that step's remedy describes. It costs this mission nothing. A release cannot publish the banner to the host landing pages without the suite passing on every host, and a README template and an image change no skill, agent, or tool behaviour the suite exercises. The banner commits land on main without the before-commit run CONTRIBUTING.md asks for. Any failure, including one with an unrelated cause, surfaces only at release time, when the work is no longer fresh. Whether the deferral leaves the mission at all depends on the release-within-mission question, since a release inside this mission would run the pre-flight here.

alternative.id: Closing agent run on all hosts

open-question.alternative: The mission runs the host suite on all three hosts (claude, antigravity, codex) once, as its last task, after every banner change under scripts/hosts/ has landed. The executing agent completes that task. It first brings each installed copy up to date with the committed tree by that host's documented install: the Claude Code directory-marketplace copy already reads the checkout, Antigravity's ~/.gemini/config/plugins/gurita is re-copied from hosts/antigravity/, and Codex is re-added from hosts/codex. It then runs the three hosts at once, as the release pre-flight does, and the task's verified bar records each host's exit status. The intermediate banner commits are not gated one by one. The final state of every host's changed trigger set passes the suite inside the mission, at the cost of one parallel run that takes as long as the slowest host. The next release's pre-flight then has a known-good baseline, and an unattended chain can finish the run without the maintainer. The agent writes into the maintainer's real home-directory installations (~/.gemini, the Codex plugin cache), and the suite deliberately leaves that work to a human. The run takes minutes of real CLI sessions on every host for a change that alters no skill, agent, or tool the suite drives. It also covers only the final state, so the CONTRIBUTING rule to run the suite before each commit touching a trigger set is met for the last commit only.

Every banner task whose commit changes a file under any scripts/hosts/<host>/ directory runs the suite on each host whose set it touches before it commits, as CONTRIBUTING.md's development rule reads literally. Each run comes after the executing agent has refreshed that host's installed copy, so the prerequisite equality check passes against the tree that task leaves. It is the only option that follows the contributor rule to the letter. Every commit on main touching a host's trigger set was verified on that host, so a revert or bisect never lands on an unchecked state. The cost multiplies by the number of tasks that touch the host directories, each costing minutes on three real CLIs plus a reinstall, and all of it guards README and image changes the suite exercises no behaviour of. It writes into the maintainer's home installations once per task. How many runs it costs depends on how the banner reaches the host trees (the banner delivery question) and how its tasks are split.

The mission runs the suite on all three hosts once, after every banner change has landed. The run is a step the maintainer performs by hand, outside any task completion, refreshing each host's installed copy first. The mission records it as a requirement to meet before finish rather than as a task an agent completes. The final state is verified on every host inside the mission, as in the agent-run option, while the home-directory installations stay under the maintainer's own hand, which is what the suite's write-nothing-to-any-installation contract expects. An unattended chain cannot reach finish without the human step. The run leaves no Task-completion commit or verified bar, so the record of it is only whatever the maintainer notes. It also still gates only the final state, not each commit.

alternative.id: Closing run on changed plugin copies

open-question.alternative: The executing agent runs the suite once, as the mission's last task, only on the hosts whose installed plugin directory the banner changes: Claude Code and Antigravity, whose plugin directory is the whole host tree and so includes the README. Codex is left out because its README, and any banner file beside it, sits at the marketplace root outside hosts/codex/plugins/gurita/, so its installed copy and the suite's prerequisite comparison are unchanged. Before the run the agent refreshes the two installed copies. It spends real runs only where the installed plugin a host loads actually differs from the last release. That cuts one host's run and one reinstall, and skips the host for which a run would re-test exactly what was last released. It departs from the documented trigger-set rule, which owes Codex a run for any change under scripts/hosts/codex/, so the next release's pre-flight still selects Codex. It holds only if the banner adds nothing under the Codex plugin directory, which depends on the banner delivery question.

alternative.id: Exempt non-runtime files from trigger sets

open-question.alternative: The mission rejects the premise that a README or image change owes a suite run. It narrows each host's trigger set to exclude files that are not part of the runtime integration, such as the definition directory's README.md and image files. The narrowing is made in both homes of the rule: CONTRIBUTING.md's Development section and the release skill's step-g diff commands. The suite is then not run for the banner, now or at the next release. It removes the cost for good, for this and every later landing-page change. The trigger sets then describe what the suite actually tests, so no future cosmetic edit owes minutes of real CLI sessions on three hosts. It widens the mission beyond the banner into the contributor rule and the maintainer-only release skill, which the goal does not mention. A path-pattern exclusion must also be kept right by hand, so a later file in a definition directory that does affect the integration could slip past it unverified.

open-question.question: Does a permanent check guard the banner once it is in place, for example a test that each of the four READMEs opens with the banner image or that every committed copy of the SVG is identical, or is the banner verified once when its tasks are completed, no test reading a README's content today?
open-question.recommendation: The one silent failure is the committed SVG drifting from the drawing it is generated from, and a test that regenerates and compares closes it the way --check closes it for hosts/; a banner dropped or displaced shows at once on the page itself, so the READMEs' opening lines stay unpinned.
open-question.alternative: A test under tests/, run by both pytest runs in CI, checks only the banner file: every committed copy parses as a well-formed SVG and all copies are byte-identical. If the art is generated by a script, it also checks that the committed SVG equals what the script produces from the plain-text drawing. Nothing checks where the READMEs place the image. Guards the one failure a reader of the page may not notice right away, copies or a generated file quietly drifting from their source, while leaving the READMEs' prose untested and free to change. What it can check depends on two sibling questions: banner delivery (whether there are several copies, and whether the build already makes them identical through --check) and banner source of truth (whether a generating script exists). If there is one file and no script, the test reduces to a well-formedness check of little value. Placement on the four pages stays unguarded.

No check is added. The banner's placement and its file are verified once, against each task's acceptance bar, when the banner tasks are completed, and nothing afterwards reads the READMEs' content or the SVG, as is the case for every README today. This is meant as never, not as postponed to a later mission. Adds nothing to the test suite or the build for a decorative image whose loss or displacement shows at once on the landing page itself. The READMEs stay free prose with no test pinning their first lines, so later edits to the page openings meet no extra gate. Nothing catches the banner being dropped or pushed below the badges by a later hand edit of the root README or a host template. If several committed copies of the SVG exist, nothing catches them drifting apart either; the three hand-kept traffic-workflow copies show that hand-kept copies rely on maintainers remembering to grep. How many copies exist is decided by the banner-delivery question.

A test under tests/, run by both pytest runs in CI, asserts that the root README and each of the three host READMEs, read from the templates under scripts/hosts/ or from the rendered trees, open with the banner image: their first non-blank element is an image whose source names the banner. Nothing checks the SVG file itself. Pins exactly what the goal promises, that the banner is the very first element on all four landing pages. It reuses the suite's existing habit of reading rendered host trees (as test_fixed_console_lines.py does) and changes no build code. It is the first test to pin README prose, so every later rework of a page opening must also update the test. It leaves the SVG copies unguarded, so if the banner-delivery question puts hand-kept copies in several definition directories, drift between them goes unseen. It also does not run in the release pre-flight, which runs --check rather than the unit suite.

A test module under tests/, run by both pytest runs in CI, combines both checks. Each of the four READMEs must open with the banner image, and every committed copy of the SVG must be well-formed and byte-identical, or equal to the generating script's output if one exists. Guards both ways the banner can silently break, displacement on a page and drift of the file, in the suite that already runs on every push, with no change to the build. Carries both costs. It is the first test pinning README prose, and its file half depends on the banner-delivery and source-of-truth siblings for what there is to compare. It is the largest test addition for a decorative asset, and it still does not run in the release pre-flight.

A new named check in scripts/build_hosts.py, run by --check in CI and in the release pre-flight, fails when a rendered host README, or the root README, does not open with the banner image. Reading the root README follows the precedent of check_root_marketplace reading a root file. Nothing checks the SVG file itself. Runs at the gate that decides what the release publishes to the three host pages, so a host tree whose README lost its banner cannot be released. It sits beside the existing tree checks rather than in the tools' test suite. It extends the build's validation from structure (placeholders, frontmatter, manifests) to the content of prose files. It also has to read the root README, which is no build input. The SVG copies stay unguarded, which matters if the banner-delivery question puts hand-kept copies in several definition directories.

alternative.id: File integrity check in the build

open-question.alternative: A new named check in scripts/build_hosts.py, run by --check in CI and in the release pre-flight, fails when the banner copies across the definition directories differ from one another or do not parse as a well-formed SVG. If the art is generated, it also fails when the committed SVG differs from the script's output. Nothing checks where the READMEs place the image. The build already reads every definition directory, so comparing the hand-kept copies there is natural. It stops a release from publishing drifted copies to the host pages. It is only meaningful if the banner-delivery question keeps one hand-made copy per definition directory. If the build copies one shared file, --check already guarantees identity; if the READMEs use an absolute URL, there is nothing to compare. It is also tied to the source-of-truth question for any regeneration part. Placement on the four pages stays unguarded.

alternative.id: Placement and integrity in the build

open-question.alternative: New named checks in scripts/build_hosts.py, run by --check in CI and in the release pre-flight, fail on both problems: when the root README or a rendered host README does not open with the banner image, and when the committed banner copies are not well-formed or not identical (or, if generated, differ from the script's output). One gate guards both ways the banner can silently break, and it is the gate every push and every release already passes. A broken banner can therefore neither land unnoticed on main nor reach the host pages. This is the largest extension of the build's check set. It brings prose-content rules and a read of the root README, which is no build input, into the build. Its file half depends on the banner-delivery and source-of-truth siblings for what there is to compare.

open-question.question: How is the banner's rendered appearance checked before it is committed, the repository holding no tool that renders an SVG: by rendering the file locally to an image that is inspected, by viewing it on GitHub after a push in both page themes, or by no rendering check beyond the file being a well-formed SVG?
open-question.applied-principle: Check tier claims against the live environment
open-question.recommendation: The local render gives the drawing agent a loop it can see before anything is committed, qlmanage on this machine having rendered a test SVG with pinned characters correctly, and the view on github.com in both themes covers what no local renderer shows, the viewer's own monospace font and the real page backgrounds.
open-question.alternative: The SVG is rendered locally to PNGs on the light and dark backgrounds and inspected before the commit, with a renderer already on the machine and nothing committed for it, and after the push to main the README pages are viewed on github.com in both themes as a final confirmation, a fix landing as a follow-up commit. Combines a fast pre-commit loop that catches most mistakes before they are public with a final check against what visitors actually see, covering the local renderer's fidelity gap. The most effort of any option, two checks for one image, and a fault only GitHub shows still reaches the public page briefly before its follow-up fix.

Before the commit, the SVG is rendered locally to a PNG with a renderer already on the machine and not added to the repository (macOS's WebKit-based qlmanage thumbnailer or ImageMagick, both present here; no rsvg-convert, Inkscape, or cairosvg is installed), composited on GitHub's light and dark page background colours, and inspected; nothing is committed for the check, and no GitHub view is part of it. Catches a wrong look before anything lands, in a fast loop that costs no push and no new dependency, and the rendered PNG is something the executing agent can itself read as an image while it iterates on the drawing. A local renderer is not what a viewer's browser on GitHub draws: text elements fall back to this machine's fonts rather than the viewer's, and ImageMagick's own SVG renderer supports less than a browser does, so a banner can pass locally and still misrender on the page; how much that gap matters depends on how the characters are drawn (text versus outlined paths), which a sibling question settles, and whose eyes judge the PNG is the drawing-approval sibling's axis.

A small script committed under scripts/ renders the SVG to PNGs on the light and dark page backgrounds, run before each commit that touches the banner and inspected by eye; it is a tool run by hand, not a test, and no GitHub view is part of the check. The check is reproducible: any later edit of the banner, by anyone, re-renders it the same way rather than relying on whatever renderer happens to be installed. Adds a tool the repository does not have today, which either brings a rendering dependency into a tooling project whose one dependency is PyYAML or shells out to a platform-specific renderer, and it carries the same local-versus-GitHub fidelity gap as any local render while leaving one more file to maintain for an image that may rarely change.

The banner is committed on a scratch branch pushed to the source repository (or opened as a pull request), and the root README and each rendered hosts/<host>/README.md are viewed on github.com in both the light and dark page themes before the change lands on main; no local render is made. Checks the real thing before it is public on the landing page: GitHub's own image serving and sanitization, in a real browser, in both themes, exactly as a visitor will see it. Needs a push and a branch outside the mission's usual commit-on-main flow, every fix costs another push-and-look round, and an unattended executing agent cannot view the page itself, so the look is judged by whoever opens the browser; a host README's relative image path resolves on the source repository's branch only if the delivery chosen by a sibling question places the file there.

The banner is committed on main as any other change, with no rendering check before the commit; once pushed, the root README and the rendered host READMEs are viewed on github.com in both page themes, and anything wrong is corrected by a follow-up commit. Fits the workflow as it runs, one commit per task on main with no extra branch or tool, while still checking the true rendered look on the page that matters. Rejects the "before it is committed" premise: a misrendered banner is public on the source repository's landing page until the fix lands, and it would ride into a release if the push-and-look step is skipped before one, which a sibling question decides whether this mission makes.

No rendering check at all: the SVG is checked only to parse as well-formed XML and its source read to confirm its colours and dimensions are the ones decided; the rendered look is never inspected before or after the commit. Costs nothing beyond what any committed file gets and needs no renderer, push, or human viewing, so an unattended execution can complete it end to end. The banner exists only to look right, and nothing confirms it does: fallback fonts misaligning the art, colours unreadable on one theme, or a wrong displayed size all ship unseen; the risk is lower only if the characters are outlined as paths, which a sibling question decides.
